why: Knowing what Verbal measures and how its three question types are built lets you recognize each format at a glance.
rule:
Verbal Reasoning tests your ability to analyze and evaluate written material, to analyze relationships among parts of sentences, and to recognize relationships among words and concepts.

About half the measure is **Reading Comprehension**: a passage with one to six questions; select one of five answers, select one or more of three, or select a sentence in the passage. The other half asks you to complete existing sentences: **Text Completion** (one to five sentences, one to three blanks) and **Sentence Equivalence** (one blank, six choices, pick two). Multi-answer questions earn no partial credit.

examples.prompt: One sentence, one blank, six choices, and you must pick two. Identify the type, then solve: "Because the argument was so ______, even the author's critics found it hard to reject." Choices: cogent, feeble, trite, compelling, murky, evasive.
steps: Type: one sentence, one blank, six choices, two answers is **Sentence Equivalence**; both picks must be right.
Signal: *so ... that even the critics found it hard to reject* means the argument was strong.
Predict *convincing*; the two closest choices are *cogent* and *compelling*.
Check: both sentences say the argument was strong; *feeble*, *trite*, *murky* and *evasive* would make it easy to reject.

trap: Treating all three types alike. In Reading Comprehension everything must come from the passage; in Text Completion and Sentence Equivalence the clues are in the sentence itself. In every multi-answer type, a partly right answer scores nothing.

checks.stem: Select one entry from the choices that best completes the text.

content.text: The lecture was so {{1}} that students who had never studied the subject followed every step.

checks.explanation: **Text Completion, one blank (five choices).** *Students who had never studied the subject followed every step*: the explanation was clear, *lucid*.

choiceExplanations.E: Wandering talks are hard to follow.
choiceExplanations.B: Technical talks are harder for beginners.
choiceExplanations.A: Dense talks are hard for beginners.

checks.stem: Select the **two** answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.

content.text: The mayor's reply was deliberately {{1}}, committing her to nothing and leaving reporters unsure of her position.

checks.explanation: **Sentence Equivalence (pick two).** *Committing to nothing* and leaving reporters unsure: *noncommittal* and *evasive*.

choiceExplanations.C: Direct; the reply left reporters unsure.
choiceExplanations.B: One-sided; the reply avoided taking a side.

checks.stem: For each blank select one entry from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

content.text: The first season of the series was {{1}} by audiences, who stayed away in droves, but the second was {{2}}, and critics now regard the show as a landmark.

checks.explanation: **Text Completion, two blanks.** *Stayed away in droves* gives *shunned*; *but* ... *landmark* gives a second season that was *a triumph*.

choiceExplanations.1C: Audiences who stayed away did not embrace it.
choiceExplanations.1A: Analyzing a show is not what staying away describes.
choiceExplanations.2A: Does not explain its landmark status.
